name: swi-prolog
why: A mature Prolog with a REPL that teaches logic programming; widely used but still an odd and rewarding language to explore.

brief.what_it_is: SWI-Prolog is an open source (BSD-2) implementation of the Prolog logic programming language, written in C and Prolog, with many extensions beyond the core language. You give it Prolog source files or type goals at its interactive top level (`?-` prompt), and it runs queries and prints answers. The README says it runs on Linux, most POSIX systems, macOS and Windows. A WASM build also exists for browsers and Node.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says development has been driven by the needs of real-world applications since 1987, and it is pitched as "Robust, mature, free. Prolog for the real world." The README lists uses including business rule validation, NLP, software verification, network configuration, robotics, graph processing, machine learning and linked data (RDF).
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals of the engine. It describes the user-facing pieces: a console REPL that works with any editor, an optional comprehensive build that adds XPCE (the GUI toolkit that provides swipl-win), PceEmacs, a source-level debugger and profiling tools, and online options (SWISH, which is sandboxed, and the WASM-based SWI-Tinker, which is not). Documentation is searchable from the prompt with apropos and help.

brief.install_notes: Installing via brew gives swipl, swipl-ld and swipl-win. The README says swipl-win (the XPCE GUI) comes in comprehensive builds, which are the default for Windows, macOS and the Linux flatpak. Source builds use CMAKE.md or the website's build page. Initialisation files are searched for in the user's config directory and the home directory (.swiplrc); the -f, -s and -g options control startup. The HTML manual sits in doc/Manual in the installation, and some packagers move it elsewhere. I did not see any account, hardware or licence-key requirement.
brief.standout: Unlike many Prolog systems, it bundles a full GUI toolkit (XPCE), an Emacs-based editor mode (PceEmacs), a source-level debugger and a WASM build that can touch the browser DOM. It is also a long-running, widely used system with many libraries. The homepage says "Join over a million users who have downloaded SWI-Prolog."
brief.status: Maintained, as far as I can tell. The homepage shows "Powered by SWI-Prolog 10.1.18", the README has an active CI badge on the master branch, and the site links a forum, a blog, a roadmap on GitHub and a commercial support company. I did not see a release date or last-commit date in the pages I read.
brief.caveats: The brew description calls it an ISO/Edinburgh-style interpreter, but the README describes it as an implementation with many extensions and does not claim ISO conformance; the writer should not repeat the ISO framing without checking. Several features need the comprehensive build (XPCE, swipl-win, PceEmacs). The online SWISH version is sandboxed and lacks modules, threads and most interfaces. Cloning the repo is awkward: fork-and-clone does not work because of git submodules. The command-line docs page includes user comments that disagree with the main text on init file lookup. Those comments are not authoritative.
quotes: Robust, mature, free. Prolog for the real world.
You can use SWI-Prolog simply at the console of your favourite OS with any editor to manage the source code.
